metadata.title: Consolidated Rail Corporation v. Gottshall, 512 U.S. 532 (1994) (No. 92-1956)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Consolidated Rail Corporation v. Gottshall

Opinion filed: 1994-06-24

Docket No.: 92-1956

Citations:
• 129 L. Ed. 2d 427
• 114 S. Ct. 2396
• 512 U.S. 532
• 1994 U.S. LEXIS 4821

Case holding summaries:
• “Because FELA is silent on the issue of negligent infliction of emotional distress, common-law principles must play a significant role in our decision.”
• noting that 16 "traditional tort concepts" include "injury" and "breach of 17 duty"
• reversing and remanding for the lower court to apply the correct legal standard in the first instance
• holding that “as part of its duty to use reasonable care in furnishing its employees with a safe place to work, a railroad has a duty under FELA to avoid subjecting its workers to negligently inflicted emotional injury” (citation and quotation marks omitted)
• rejecting Carlisle's claim because it alleged "that he had been given too much not too dangerous work to do"
• finding no support for the imposition "of a duty to avoid creating a stressful work environment"
• also noting that "[b]ehind these limitations lie a variety of policy considerations, many of them based on the fundamental differences between emotional and physical injuries"
• suggesting that the employer becomes liable based on the "emotional injury caused by the apprehension of physical impact," regardless of whether actual physical contact occurs
• reviewing the history and general principles of FELA
• describing FELA's "central focus on physical perils"
• defining negligently inflicted emotional distress as "mental or emotional harm (such as fright or anxiety) that is caused by the negligence of another and that is not directly brought about by a physical injury"
• "That FELA is to be liberally construed, however, does not mean that it is a workers' compensation statute."
• "[T]hese terms traditionally have been used to describe sensations stemming directly from a physical injury or condition" (internal quotation marks omitted)
• stating that through the Federal Employers' Liability Act "Congress crafted a federal remedy [for railroad workers] that shifted part of the 'human overhead' of doing business from employees to their employers"
• no liability under the fela for emotional injury unless the victim also suffers physical injury
• adopting zone of danger test to “limit[ ] recovery for emotional injury to those plaintiffs who sustain a physical impact as a result of a defendant’s negligent conduct, or who are placed in immediate risk of physical harm by that conduct”
• “The injury we deal with here is mental or emotional harm (such as fright or anxiety) . . . .”
• “If one takes a broad enough view, all consequences of a negligent act, no matter how removed in time or space, may be foreseen.”
• noting that Conrail "wisely declined" to attack Gottshall's claim as fraudulent
• discussing "physical impact," "zone of danger," and "relative bystander" tests
• suggesting a distinction between claims for "pure emotional injury" and those involving "physical symptoms in addition to . . . severe psychological illness"
• preferring the zone of danger test to the impact rule, because, inter alia, the latter "has considerably less support in the current state of the common law" than the former
• "[P]olicy considerations mandat[e] that infinite liability be avoided by restrictions that . . . narrow the class of potential plaintiffs"
• "[T]here are clear judicial days on which a court can foresee forever and thus determine liability but none on which that foresight alone provides a socially and judicially acceptable limit on recovery"
• disallowing prejudgment interest under FELA in large part because such interest was unavailable at common law when FELA was enacted
• "[N]othing in either the language or the legislative history discloses expressly any intent to exclude from the Act's coverage any injury resulting `in whole or in part from the negligence' of the carrier"
• discussing tort claims brought under the Federal Employers’ Liability Act
• “[A]lthough common-law principles are not necessarily dispositive of questions arising under FELA, unless they are expressly rejected in the text of the statute, they are entitled to great weight in our analysis.”
• “[FELA] is founded on common-law concepts of negligence and injury, subject to such qualifications as Congress has imported into those terms[.]”
• “FELA does not make the employer the insurer of the safety of his employees while they are on duty. The basis of his liability is his negligence, not the fact that injuries occur.”
• reversing and remanding for the lower court to apply the correct legal standard in the first instance
• reversing and remanding for the lower court to apply the correct legal standard in the first instance
• stating that under FELA, courts should apply the traditional elements of negligence
• railroad employees may recover for emotional damages caused by an employer's negligent conduct that imminently threatens an employee with physical impact, but not for emotional injuries stemming from a stressful working environment
• “[W]hen Congress enacted FELA in 3 1908, its attention was focused primarily upon injuries and death resulting from 4 accidents on interstate railroads.” (internal quotation marks and citation omitted)
• "[w]hether plaintiff is within a zone of danger is an objective inquiry"
• "Under the physical impact test, a plaintiff seeking damages for emotional injury stemming from a negligent act must have contemporaneously sustained a physical impact (no matter how slight) or injury due to the defendant's conduct." (emphasis supplied
• "Under the physical impact test, a plaintiff seeking damages for emotional injury stemming from a negligent act must have contemporaneously sustained a physical impact (no matter how slight) or injury due to the defendant's conduct." (emphasis supplied)
• “Only to the extent of … explicit statutory alterations is FELA an avowed departure from the rules of the common law.”
• “We have liberally construed FELA to further Congress’ remedial goal.”
• “relaxed standard of causation applies under FELA”
• “Because FELA is silent on the issue of negligent infliction of emotional distress, common-law principles must play a significant role in our decision.”
• reversing and remanding for the lower court to apply the correct legal standard in the first instance
• "Cognizant of the physical dangers of railroading that resulted in the death or maiming of thousands of workers each year, Congress crafted a federal remedy that shifted part of the `human overhead' of doing business from employees to their employers."
• cataloging states' bystander recovery tests
• holding that common law principles are entitled to great weight in FELA analysis unless expressly rejected in text of statute
• "zone of danger test . . . is consistent with FELA's central focus on physical perils"
• employer should be liable for "emotional injury caused by the apprehension of physical impact"
• “The injury we deal with here is mental or emotional harm . . . that is caused by the negligence of another and that is not directly brought about by a physical injury . . . .”
• railroad worker who suffered nervous breakdown allegedly due to stressful working environment could not recover from railroad under FELA for negligent infliction of emotional distreess; there was no common-law basis for recognizing right to recovery on those facts
